title: He Was Last After Six Rounds. Four Wins Later, Praggnanandhaa Had the Norway Chess Title.
excerpt: The 20-year-old from Chennai became the first Indian to win Norway Chess, beating Magnus Carlsen twice along the way in what he calls the biggest win of his career.
body:
On June 1, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu called his mother from Oslo. He was languishing near the bottom of the Norway Chess standings, having lost three of his first six classical games. His mother told him what mothers tell their sons: *It's a new month. You'll play well.*

Four days later, having won four consecutive classical games against some of the strongest players alive, the 20-year-old from Chennai lifted the Norway Chess trophy — the first Indian ever to do so.

"I think this is the biggest win of my career," Praggnanandhaa said afterward. "Winning this is more special, and Magnus was there."

The comeback is almost impossible to overstate. After losing to Wesley So in round six, Praggnanandhaa found himself in last place, 5.5 points behind the leader. What followed was a run of classical chess victories that even Carlsen called "pretty insane" — wins over Alireza Firouzja, Carlsen himself, World Champion D Gukesh, and finally Vincent Keymer in the decisive final round.

The critical game came on Friday against Keymer, who had been unbeaten in classical play. Playing with the white pieces, Praggnanandhaa built pressure methodically rather than lunging for tactical fireworks. When Keymer slipped with **30...h5?**, leaving a gaping hole on g5, Praggnanandhaa pounced with **31.Rb8+** and converted flawlessly.

"I couldn't think anymore — I was just making moves with my hand!" he confessed about the final moments.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZQm7aozgF4/

The mathematics going into the final round had been stark. Wesley So led with 15.5 points and needed only a classical win against Firouzja to clinch the title. So drew in classical and won the armageddon tiebreaker, earning 1.5 points for a total of 17. But Praggnanandhaa's full 3-point classical victory took him to 18, one clear of So.

"Five days ago I would give a 0.1% chance that he would win four in a row, but it happened, it's crazy!" So said. "There's nothing really Firouzja and I could do."

The feat is made more remarkable by who Praggnanandhaa beat along the way. He defeated Carlsen twice in classical chess during the tournament — only the second Indian to do so in a single event, after Viswanathan Anand beat Carlsen twice at Linares in 2007. Carlsen, the seven-time Norway Chess champion and the player the tournament was essentially built around, took the result with characteristic candor: "He is an incredible fighter, and it's fun to see him get rewarded for that."

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian chess community worldwide, Praggnanandhaa's triumph is the latest evidence of a generational surge that began with Anand and has accelerated dramatically. Gukesh became the youngest world champion in history last year. Praggnanandhaa's sister Vaishali won the Candidates Tournament. And now Praggnanandhaa has conquered Norway Chess, the only classical event Carlsen still plays.

The win also helped Praggnanandhaa cross back above 2750 in the live ratings after a turbulent year that saw him drop from 2790. He has spoken openly about the disappointment of the FIDE Candidates going badly after two years of focused preparation. His sister's success cushioned the blow, he said, and his new approach is working: "I don't want to think about the next Candidates already at this point — I just want to chill and enjoy the games."

The final standings: Praggnanandhaa 18 points, Wesley So 17, Alireza Firouzja 15.5, Magnus Carlsen 13, Vincent Keymer 12.5, D Gukesh 11.5. In the women's event, Bibisara Assaubayeva clinched the title with a round to spare, while India's Divya Deshmukh and Koneru Humpy competed in the six-player field.

For Gukesh, the tournament ended in last place — more food for thought in a year when he'll defend his world championship title. Carlsen lost more rating points than anyone but remains world number one, approaching 15 years unbroken at the top.

Praggnanandhaa, though, is the story. Last place to first. Four wins in a row. The first Indian name on the Norway Chess trophy.

His mother knew something, he guesses.
